questions.question: What are the most useful Array methods in Ruby?
questions.title: Essential Ruby Array Methods
questions.direct_answer: Arrays are ordered lists, and Ruby's Enumerable gives them powerful methods. The essentials: map/collect (transform each element -> new array: [1,2,3].map{|n| n*2} == [2,4,6]); select/filter (keep matching -> new array: [1,2,3,4].select{|n| n.even?} == [2,4]); reject (drop matching); find/detect (first match: [1,2,3].find{|n| n>2} == 3); each (iterate, no return); reduce/inject (fold to one value: [1,2,3].reduce(0){|s,n| s+n} == 6); sort/sort_by (order); flatten (nested -> flat); uniq (dedupe); include? (membership). map vs each: map returns a new array; each returns the original. Use the bang versions (map!, select!) to mutate in place. These compose: nums.select{|n| n.even?}.map{|n| n*10}.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know map/select/reduce/find/sort and the map-vs-each distinction (map returns a new array; each doesn't).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using each when you want a transformed array (it returns the original, not the result), or forgetting map! mutates in place.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Arrays: map (transform), select/reject (filter), find (first match), reduce (fold), sort/sort_by, each (iterate), uniq, include?. map returns a new array; each doesn't. Bang versions mutate.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Define Essential Ruby Array Methods simply, show a small example, and mention the main trade-off or edge case.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: map/collect transforms each element to a new array; select/filter keeps matches.
reject drops matches; find/detect returns the first match (or nil).
reduce/inject folds to one value (e.g. a sum); sort/sort_by orders.
map vs each: map returns a new array; each returns the original (no transform).
Bang versions (map!, select!) mutate in place; methods compose (select.map).

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Arrays are ordered lists, and Ruby's Enumerable gives them powerful methods. The essentials: map or collect (transform each element to a new array: 1 2 3 map n times 2 equals 2 4 6); select or filter (keep matching to a new array: 1 2 3 4 select n even equals 2 4); reject (drop matching); find or detect (first match: 1 2 3 find n greater than 2 equals 3); each (iterate, no return); reduce or inject (fold to one value: 1 2 3 reduce 0 sum equals 6); sort or sort_by (order); flatten (nested to flat); uniq (dedupe); include question (membership). map versus each: map returns a new array; each returns the original. Use the bang versions (map!, select!) to mutate in place. These compose: nums select n even map n times 10. A common mistake is using each when you want a transformed array, because each returns the original, not the result, and forgetting that map! mutates in place.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Arrays are ordered lists, and Ruby's Enumerable gives them powerful methods.

The essentials: map/collect (transform each element -> new array: [1,2,3].map{|n| n*2} == [2,4,6]); select/filter (keep matching -> new array: [1,2,3,4].select{|n| n.even?} == [2,4]); reject (drop matching); find/detect (first match: [1,2,3].find{|n| n>2} == 3); each (iterate, no return); reduce/inject (fold to one value: [1,2,3].reduce(0){|s,n| s+n} == 6); sort/sort_by (order); flatten (nested -> flat); uniq (dedupe); include?

(membership). map vs each: map returns a new array; each returns the original. Use the bang versions (map!, select!) to mutate in place. These compose: nums.select{|n| n.even?}.map{|n| n*10}.

A common mistake is using each when you want a transformed array (it returns the original, not the result), or forgetting map! mutates in place.

sections.title: Array Method Families
sections.content:
map (transform), select/reject (filter), find (first), reduce (fold), sort, each (iterate).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[array] --> M[map: transform -> new]
  A --> S[select: filter -> new]
  A --> F[find: first match]
  A --> R[reduce: fold to one]
  M --> C[compose: select.map]
```

sections.title: Array methods
sections.content:
```ruby
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]

nums.map { |n| n * 2 }        # [2, 4, 6, 8]   (new array)
nums.select { |n| n.even? }   # [2, 4]         (keep matches)
nums.reject { |n| n.even? }  # [1, 3]         (drop matches)
nums.find { |n| n > 2 }       # 3              (first match; nil if none)
nums.reduce(0) { |s, n| s + n } # 10          (fold to one value)
nums.sort                    # [1, 2, 3, 4]
nums.sort_by { |n| -n }       # [4, 3, 2, 1]   (sort by key)
nums.each { |n| puts n }     # prints 1..4; returns original (not a new array)
nums.uniq                    # dedupe
nums.include?(3)             # true (membership)
nums.flatten                 # [[1,2],[3]] -> [1,2,3]

# map vs each: map returns a NEW array; each returns the ORIGINAL.
[1,2,3].each { |n| n * 10 }  # returns [1,2,3]  (NOT [10,20,30])
[1,2,3].map  { |n| n * 10 }  # returns [10,20,30]

# Bang versions mutate in place:
a = [1,2,3]; a.map! { |n| n*10 }; a  # [10,20,30]

# Composition (read left to right):
nums.select { |n| n.even? }.map { |n| n * 10 }  # [20, 40]
```
